title: EAST — Four Simple Ways to Apply Behavioural Insights https://www.bi.team/publications/east-four-simple-ways-to-apply-behavioural-insights/
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), October 22, 2025 — original paper:
summary: Barton covers the Behavioural Insights Team's updated EAST guide, which distills behavioural-science research into four principles for encouraging any desired behaviour: make it Easy, Attractive, Social, and Timely. Drawing on examples spanning US university students, TB patients in Moldova, mathematics teachers, and factory workers, the guide shows that reducing friction (simplifying an application process lifted attendance from 28% to 36%), using sensible defaults (95% opt-in when a service was automatic rather than opt-in), and loss-framed incentives (a bonus given upfront and clawed back if goals aren't met) all reliably move behaviour. Barton translates these into classroom terms: streamline the effort required for high-value student tasks, use defaults deliberately, frame incentives as losses rather than gains, and use implementation-intention planning and 'fresh start' moments to help students bridge the gap between intention and action. He also flags the guide's own caution that context matters and that the behavioural-science field has faced a replication crisis, so any EAST-inspired intervention needs local evaluation rather than blind import.
points: Reducing friction for a desired task has outsized effects — simplifying the university application process alone lifted attendance among under-represented students from 28% to 36%.
Defaults are powerful: automatically enrolling parents in a text-message progress service produced 95% uptake, far above what leaders expected from an opt-in system.
Loss-framed incentives (a bonus paid upfront and forfeited if goals aren't met) improved student maths scores more than standard end-of-year gain incentives, with effects lasting over five years.

Helping students form specific implementation-intention plans — identifying barriers and deciding exactly when and where they'll act — closes the gap between wanting to do something and actually doing it.
The guide's own caution applies to any classroom use: behavioural science has a replication crisis, so EAST-style interventions need context-specific evaluation, not blind copying.
quotes: If you want to encourage a behaviour, make it easy, attractive, social and timely (EAST).
One study found that simply automating and streamlining parts of the university application process increased attendance rates from 28% to 36%.
For example, assuming parents are automatically signed up for a text message service detailing student progress resulted in a 95% enrollment rate, significantly higher than what leaders expected.

For teachers, the use of loss-framed incentives (giving a bonus upfront that must be returned if goals are not met) was more effective at improving student mathematics scores than standard end-of-year gain incentives, with positive effects lasting over five years.
Teachers must recognise that context remains crucial; interventions that are successful elsewhere may not work in a classroom.
The field faces a replication crisis, meaning results might fail to hold up to scrutiny.
